title: switch and restore
summary: Move between branches with git switch, and throw away changes in the index or working tree with git restore.

steps.title: switch: change where HEAD points
body: git switch feature          # HEAD -> feature; working tree now matches feature's tip
git switch -c bugfix        # create a branch here and switch to it
git switch -                # back to the previous branch

Switching updates the **working tree and index** to the target commit's snapshot. Your uncommitted changes come along if they do not clash; if they would be overwritten, Git refuses and tells you to commit or stash first. It never silently destroys work.

> **Tip:** `git checkout` is the older command that does both switching and restoring. You will see it in docs and scripts (`git checkout -b bugfix` = `git switch -c bugfix`). The newer `switch` and `restore` split those jobs so the dangerous one is explicit.

steps.prompt: You have an unstaged edit to `README.md`, and `README.md` is identical on `main` and `feature`. You run `git switch feature`. What happens?
options: The switch succeeds and your edit is still in the working tree
Git refuses because you have uncommitted changes
Your edit is committed to `main` first
steps.explain: Git only refuses when a file you changed differs between the two branches, because switching would overwrite your edit. Otherwise local changes ride along.

steps.title: restore: copy a file back
body: `git restore` copies a file **from** somewhere **to** somewhere:
git restore --staged f        git restore f
| `git restore f` | discard unstaged edits: copy f from the **index** to the working tree |
| `git restore --staged f` | unstage: copy f from **HEAD** into the index (your edits on disk stay) |
| `git restore --source=HEAD~2 f` | bring back f as it was two commits ago, into the working tree |
`git restore f` throws your edits away for good: they were never committed, so not even the reflog can bring them back.

steps.prompt: `a.cs` is committed as `v1`. You change it to `v2`, run `git add a.cs`, then change it to `v3`. You then run `git restore a.cs`. What does `git status -s` print?
code: # a.cs: HEAD=v1, then edited to v2, added, edited to v3
steps.explain: `git restore a.cs` copies the **index** version (`v2`) over the working tree, discarding `v3`. The staged change from v1 to v2 remains: `M` in the left column only.

steps.prompt: Same starting point (`HEAD=v1`, index `v2`, disk `v3`). This time you run `git restore --staged a.cs`. What does `git status -s` print?
steps.explain: Unstaging copies HEAD's `v1` into the index. The working tree still has `v3`, which now differs only from the index: ` M`.

steps.prompt: Match the goal to the command.
pairs: Undo `git add` but keep my edits
Throw away my unsaved experiment in a file
Get the version from last week's commit
Start a new branch from here
Go back to the branch I was just on

steps.prompt: Can you get the work back afterwards?
items: Commits on a branch you switched away from
A committed file you deleted with `rm`
steps.explain: Anything ever committed can be recovered. Changes that only lived in the working tree are not in Git's database, so discarding them is permanent.

steps.title: Model add and restore
prompt: Model the three commands that copy a single file between areas. Write `Run(string command, head, index, work)` that changes the dictionaries in place:
If the source does not contain the file, **remove** it from the destination (that is how a deletion is staged or a new file unstaged).
starter: static void Run(string command, Dictionary<string, string> head, Dictionary<string, string> index, Dictionary<string, string> work)
solution: static void Run(string command, Dictionary<string, string> head, Dictionary<string, string> index, Dictionary<string, string> work)
void Copy(Dictionary<string, string> from, Dictionary<string, string> to)
if (from.TryGetValue(file, out var v)) to[file] = v; else to.Remove(file);
hints: `command.Split(' ')`: the file is the last part.
Write one helper that copies a key from one dictionary to another, or removes it if the source lacks it.
Decide by `parts[1]` (`add` or `restore`) and whether `parts[2]` is `--staged`.
template: string dojoS(Dictionary<string, string> d) => string.Join(",", d.OrderBy(k => k.Key).Select(k => k.Key + "=" + k.Value));
Run("git restore a", dh, di, dw);
Run("git restore --staged a", dh, di, dw);
Dojo.Eq("...and leaves the working tree alone", "a=v2", dojoS(dw));
Run("git add a", dh, di, dw);
Dojo.Eq("add stages the working tree", "a=v2", dojoS(di));
Run("git restore --staged new", nh, ni, nw);
Dojo.Eq("unstaging a new file removes it from the index", "", dojoS(ni));
Dojo.Eq("...but keeps it on disk", "new=x", dojoS(nw));
